title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's presentiment did in fact come true. The next day, during the service at the palace church for the Emperor's birthday, Prince Volkonski was called out of the church and handed a dispatch from Prince Kutuzov. It was Kutuzov's report, written at Tatarinova on the day of the battle. Kutuzov wrote that the Russians had not given up a step, that the French had lost far more men than we had, and that he was writing in haste from the battlefield before he could gather full information. It followed that there must have been a victory. And at once, without leaving the church, they gave thanks to the Creator for His help and for the victory.

Anna Pavlovna's presentiment had been proved right, and all that morning a joyously festive mood reigned in the city. Everyone took the victory to have been complete, and some even spoke of Napoleon having been captured, of his deposition and of the choice of a new ruler for France.

It is very hard for events to be reflected in their real strength and completeness amid the conditions of court life, far from the scene of action. General events involuntarily gather around some particular incident. So now the courtiers' pleasure rested as much on the news having arrived on the Emperor's birthday as on the victory itself. It was like a successfully arranged surprise. Kutuzov's report mentioned the Russian losses, among them the names of Tuchkov, Bagration and Kutaysov. In Petersburg society this sad side of the affair again involuntarily centered on a single incident: Kutaysov's death. Everybody knew him, the Emperor liked him, and he was young and interesting. That day everyone greeted each other with the words:
"What a wonderful coincidence! Right during the service. But what a loss Kutaysov is! How sorry I am!"
"What did I tell you about Kutuzov?" Prince Vasili said now, with a prophet's pride. "I always said he was the only man capable of defeating Napoleon."
But the next day no news came from the army, and the public mood turned anxious. The courtiers suffered because of the suffering that the suspense caused the Emperor.

"Imagine the Emperor's position!" they said. And instead of praising Kutuzov as they had the day before, they blamed him for the Emperor's anxiety. That day Prince Vasili no longer boasted of his protégé Kutuzov, but kept silent whenever the commander in chief was mentioned. Moreover, toward evening, as if everything conspired to make Petersburg society anxious and uneasy, a terrible piece of news was added. Countess Helene Bezukhova had suddenly died of that terrible illness it had been so agreeable to mention. Officially, at large gatherings, everyone said that Countess Bezukhova had died of a terrible attack of angina pectoris. In intimate circles, though, people gave details. The private physician of the Queen of Spain had prescribed small doses of a certain drug to produce a certain effect. But Helene was tormented because the old count suspected her, and because her husband, to whom she had written (that wretched, profligate Pierre), had not replied. So she had suddenly taken a very large dose of the drug, and had died in agony before anyone could help her. It was said that Prince Vasili and the old count had turned on the Italian, but he had produced such letters from the unfortunate dead woman that they dropped the matter at once.
Talk in general centered on three melancholy facts: the Emperor's lack of news, the loss of Kutaysov and the death of Helene.

On the third day after Kutuzov's report, a country gentleman arrived from Moscow, and the news that Moscow had been surrendered to the French spread through the whole town. This was terrible! What a position for the Emperor to be in! Kutuzov was a traitor. And Prince Vasili, during the visits of condolence paid to him on his daughter's death, spoke of Kutuzov, whom he had praised before (in his grief he could be excused for forgetting what he had said). He said that nothing else could be expected from a blind and depraved old man.
"I only wonder that the fate of Russia could have been entrusted to such a man."
As long as this news remained unofficial, it was possible to doubt it. But the next day the following communication arrived from Count Rostopchin:

Prince Kutuzov's adjutant has brought me a letter in which he demands police officers to guide the army onto the Ryazan road. He writes that he is abandoning Moscow with regret. Sire! Kutuzov's action decides the fate of the capital and of your empire! Russia will shudder to learn that the city has been abandoned, the city in which her greatness is centered and in which the ashes of your ancestors lie! I shall follow the army. I have had everything removed, and all that remains for me is to weep over the fate of my fatherland.
On receiving this dispatch, the Emperor sent Prince Volkonski to Kutuzov with the following rescript:

Prince Michael Ilarionovich! Since the twenty-ninth of August I have received no communication from you. Yet on the first of September I received, from the commander in chief of Moscow via Yaroslavl, the sad news that you and the army have decided to abandon Moscow. You can imagine for yourself the effect this news has had on me, and your silence adds to my astonishment. I am sending this by Adjutant-General Prince Volkonski, to hear from you the situation of the army and the reasons that have led you to this melancholy decision.
